newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurostocks fall back as correction fears grow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurostocks fall back as correction fears grow.

text.p: European stock markets fell back on Wednesday as a half-hearted rally petered out due to fears that the great correction is still far from over despite a steadier overnight performance on Wall Street.

Early predictions that only the brave would buy proved correct by the middle of the afternoon. Among leading European markets, only Germany's DAX index managed to hold on to the modest morning gains while London and Paris turned down again.
Wall Street encouraged the early European rally as the Dow Jones Industrial average closed up 27.57 points at 6,611.05 on Tuesday after losing almost 300 points in the previous two sessions.
But with fears growing of more U.S. interest rate rises, the outlook for Wall Street was less rosy on Wednesday.

"We'll see a mixed to slightly stronger opening but I don't think there will be any conviction or follow-through to the little rally we had yesterday," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood in New York.
Germany's DAX index closed floor trade up just 5.98 points at 3,301.91 after climbing around 20 points earlier.

But after floor trade closed, the gloom which pushed the German market down almost four percent on Tuesday returned. By mid afternoon the IBIS DAX index measuring electronic trade was down 62.70 points or 1.91 percent at 3,218.76.
Other markets painted a similar picture. London's FTSE-100 index was down 5.6 points at 4,242.5 and the Paris CAC-40 lost 28.29 points or 1.1 percent to 2,553.53.
The question everyone tried to answer was how much further the correction to the bull run would go.
Strategist David Aserkoff of Credit Suisse First Boston was more optimistic than most, although he has advised clients to raise cash levels at the expense of equities.
"I'd say we're at or very close to the end of the correction in the U.S. and in U.K. and European markets," said Aserkoff, who cut his mid-year target for the FTSE 100 to 4,200 from 4,425.
"But just because they stop going down doesn't mean they'll start going up," he added. "The ongoing potential for the Fed to tighten further will bedevil the markets through the second quarter."
Chris Chaitow, technical analyst at Robert Fleming Securities, was more gloomy about the FTSE which has lost around four percent in the past four weeks from its intra-day record of 4,466.
"It could now go down to 3,800," he said, adding that the market's fortunes would be largely dictated by Wall Street.
"The Dow is still looking vulnerable. Some people are talking about it losing four or five hundred more points," said one London dealer.
One man will play a leading role in deciding whether the plunge is a blip on an upward graph or the end to the bull run -- U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

The U.S. central bank has already raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in a pre-emptive strike against inflation. The March rise was widely expected but now investors are beginning to speculate that the Fed might tighten policy again in May.
That could put another nail in the coffin for stocks.

The market is awaiting U.S. employment data at the end of the week for any further signs of inflationary pressures which might prompt Greenspan to try to cool the economy. "A bad payrolls number could really hurt and so everyone is wary," one dealer said.
On the foreign exchange market, the dollar was steady against the mark but weaker against the yen, although well above overnight lows at around 121.35 yen.
It fell overnight after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Japan had made progress in cutting its trade surplus but it was important that it was not reversed.

Dealers were nervous as Rubin will visit Tokyo on Friday. "There are fears in the market that the U.S. might re-think the strong dollar policy and that has depressed sentiment for dollar bulls," said Klaus Kusber, foreign exchange analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
Rubin was due to give a speech at 1730 GMT on Wednesday in Washington on his upcoming meeting with finance ministers at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation group.
"The market will be nervous. Japanese trade is coming back, very quickly, into market focus," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
At mid-afternoon, the dollar was at 122.35 yen, down from 122.60 at the European close on Tuesday. It firmed to 1.6717 marks from 1.6699.
CURRENCIES AT 1330 GMT
The dollar was at 1.6717 marks and 122.35 yen compared with 1.6699 and 122.60 in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1330 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 5.6 points, or 0.13 percent, at 4,242.5
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 28.29 points, or 1.10 percent, at 2,553.53.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed up 5.98 points, or 0.18 percent, at 3,301.91. In later electronic trade, the IBIS index was down 62.70 points or 1.91 percent at 3,218.76.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $350.70 an ounce in thre afternoon, compared with a morning fixing of $350.70 and Tuesday's close of $350.45. Silver was two cents lower at $5.02.
